# `config/mcp.json` — MCP servers

**Generated by the installer. Gitignored.** Built from `config/mcp.default.json`, which ships:

```json
{ "mcpServers": {}, "settings": { "hostConfigDiscovery": "off", "directTools": false } }
```

**No MCP servers ship with this repository.** They are per-user by nature — they carry your
credentials, your hosts and your tool surface. What ships is the machinery: the vendored adapter,
the project trust gate, the environment-minimising stdio wrapper, and the approval ledger. Read
this page before you expect a server to start, because the defaults are deny-shaped and that is
intentional.

The installer's MCP step offers exactly two servers from `config/mcp.example.json` — `context7` and
`playwright` — and **defaults to neither**. Whatever you pick is written here. If `config/mcp.json`
already exists when you re-run, the step stands down entirely and says so: the file is yours and the
installer will not edit it.

Hand edits are therefore safe. What a hand edit does not survive is a fresh clone, where only the
`.default.json` half exists — so a server you want on every machine belongs in
`config/mcp.default.json` as well.

`config/mcp.example.json` is a **template that is never loaded**. Copy entries out of it.

---

## Server entries

### HTTP server

```json
"context7": {
  "url": "https://mcp.context7.com/mcp",
  "headers": { "CONTEXT7_API_KEY": "${CONTEXT7_API_KEY}" },
  "lifecycle": "lazy",
  "directTools": true
}
```

### stdio server

```json
"playwright": {
  "command": "mcp-stdio-guard",
  "args": ["npx", "-y", "@playwright/mcp", "--headless"],
  "env": {
    "MCP_STDIO_EXTRA_ENV": "PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH",
    "PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH": "${HOME}/.cache/ms-playwright"
  },
  "lifecycle": "lazy"
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `url` | HTTP transport |
| `command` / `args` | stdio transport. **Put `mcp-stdio-guard` first** — see below |
| `headers` | `${VAR}` expansion. Credentials go here as references, never as values |
| `env` | environment for a stdio child |
| `lifecycle` | `lazy` starts the server on first use instead of at session start |
| `directTools` | per-server override of the global setting |

!!! danger "Wrap every stdio server you did not write yourself"
    A stdio MCP server is a **child process that inherits your environment** — every API key,
    every token you have exported for anything else. `config/bin/mcp-stdio-guard` re-execs the real
    command through `env -i` with an explicit baseline allowlist:

    ```text
    HOME LOGNAME PATH SHELL TERM USER LANG LC_ALL TMPDIR
    NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS HTTPS_PROXY HTTP_PROXY NO_PROXY https_proxy http_proxy no_proxy
    ```

    Anything else the server genuinely needs is named explicitly in `MCP_STDIO_EXTRA_ENV`, as the
    `playwright` example does. That is the whole mechanism: an allowlist you can read in one line,
    not a denylist you have to keep current.

    Omitting the wrapper is not a small convenience. It hands your entire credential set to code
    installed by `npx -y`.

---

## `settings`

### `hostConfigDiscovery`

Ships **`"off"`**.

Other agent tools on the same machine keep their own MCP server lists. `hostConfigDiscovery` decides
whether PI adopts them. `"off"` means: **everything you get is what is written in
`config/mcp.json`**, and nothing appears because some other program on your laptop knows about it.

**Who would change it:** somebody who genuinely wants one canonical MCP list maintained elsewhere.

**What breaks:** turning it on makes your tool surface a function of software you did not configure
here, changing under you when that other tool updates. It also silently widens what the agent can
reach, which is exactly the class of change that should be visible in a diff.

### `directTools`

Ships **`false`**.

`false` routes an MCP server's tools through a single namespaced entry point. `true` flattens them
into the top-level tool list.

**Who would change it:** set `"directTools": true` **per server** for the two or three whose tools
you use constantly — flattening makes them cheaper for the model to reach and better described.

**What breaks:** flattening everything inflates the tool schema, which is part of the preamble on
**every** request. A dozen MCP servers flattened is a permanent context tax you pay per turn and
notice as a mysteriously large preamble in `/context`. Per-server, not globally.

---

## The project trust gate

The vendored adapter carries a **local patch at `getConfigSources()`**: a server defined by a
*project* — `.mcp.json` or `.pi/mcp.json` inside a repository you opened — is **dropped unless it
has been approved**, keyed on the project path **and** the sha256 digest of those files.

```bash
pi-mcp-approve <project-dir>            # show the config, then confirm interactively
pi-mcp-approve <project-dir> --yes      # approve without the prompt, for a scripted install
pi-mcp-approve --list                   # print the ledger
pi-mcp-approve --status <project-dir>   # current verdict, changes nothing
```

The ledger is `~/.config/pi-config/mcp-approvals.jsonl`, mode `0600`, append-only; the last line for
a directory wins. To revoke, delete the matching line.

!!! danger "Being in a trusted root grants the right to RUN there, never to DEFINE MCP servers"
    `config/trusted-roots.json` and this ledger are separate gates on purpose. Cloning a repository
    into a trusted root must not silently authorise it to spawn processes on your machine with your
    environment. Approval is per project **and per content digest**: if the project's MCP config
    changes, the approval no longer matches and it is denied again.

**Exit codes:** `0` approved / clean, `1` refused or aborted, `2` the tool could not run.

---

## Why the adapter is vendored in-tree

`pi-packages/pi-mcp-adapter/` is third-party source committed into this repository rather than
installed into `node_modules/`, and the reason is the patch above. The upstream package resolves
its config sources in a way that cannot be intercepted from outside the module — there is no hook,
no option and no wrapper position that sees project sources before they are merged. The gate has to
live inside `getConfigSources()` or it does not exist.

Vendoring makes that patch visible in a diff and re-applicable on every version bump, instead of
being a `postinstall` script rewriting somebody else's code. Full attribution, licence and the
patch's behavioural difference from upstream: [Third-party components](../reference/third-party.md).

---

## Verifying a change

```bash
pi-mcp-approve --list        # what the ledger says
```

In a session, `/doctor`'s `D-07` reports any MCP server name mentioned in instruction text that is
not declared in `config/mcp.json` — the usual cause of "why can't the agent see my server".

A `lazy` server that has never been used has never been started, so its absence from the tool list
until first use is expected, not a fault.
